stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the office due to progressive discoloration of and occasional discomfort in his lower extremities.  The patient reports no chronic medical conditions but has not seen a physician for many years.  He works as a long-haul truck driver.  The patient smokes a half-pack of cigarettes daily.  Vital signs are within normal limits.  Lower extremity examination findings shown in the exhibit are present bilaterally.  Which of the following histopathologic changes is most likely present in the affected regions of this patient's lower extremities?​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌

options.label: A
options.text: Cellular extravasation from dilated veins and dermal fibrosis

options.label: C
options.text: Hyalinization and obliteration of arterioles with dermal thickening

options.label: E
options.text: Septal panniculitis containing granulomas with giant cells

explanation:
This patient's physical examination shows progressive reddish-brown discoloration of the lower extremities with skin thickening in the ankle region.  These findings are consistent with stasis dermatitis due to chronic venous insufficiency (CVI).

CVI is caused by chronic lower extremity venous hypertension, which often results from venous stasis (in this patient's case, due to prolonged sitting while driving a truck).  The consequent structural damage (eg, vessel wall weakening leading to dilated veins and incompetent venous valves) and inflammatory mediator release (exacerbated by this patient's smoking, an important CVI risk factor) lead to abnormal vascular permeability.  The result is extravasation of fluid, blood cells, and proteolytic enzymes into the interstitial space:

  • Extravasated fluid manifests as edema that initially develops in the feet and progresses proximally over time.

  • Extravasated erythrocytes are broken down, producing hemosiderin that deposits in the dermis and causes reddish-brown skin discoloration (eg, stasis dermatitis).

  • Activated leukocytes release transforming growth factor beta, leading to dermal fibrosis and woody thickening (ie, induration); in severe cases, lipodermatosclerosis can occur, causing leg disfiguration.

  • Proteolytic enzymes cause tissue damage that can contribute to ulcer formation (classically in the medial malleolar region).

CVI is often diagnosed clinically when classic manifestations of the disease are present; duplex ultrasonography showing venous reflux can also be used to confirm the diagnosis.

(Choice B)  Excessive dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans is present in pretibial myxedema, a manifestation of Graves disease.  However, exophthalmos, a diffuse goiter, and findings of hyperthyroidism (eg, heat intolerance) would be expected.

(Choice C)  Hyalinization and obliteration of arterioles with dermal thickening occur in systemic sclerosis (SSc), an autoimmune disease characterized by widespread fibrosis in multiple organ systems.  In contrast to CVI, SSc usually affects the hands and face first.  In addition, most patients with SSc exhibit Raynaud phenomenon, and extradermal manifestations (eg, esophageal dysmotility, interstitial lung disease) are common.

(Choice D)  Occlusion of lymphatic channels due to compression, obliteration, or infiltration (eg, malignancy, radiation, infection) can lead to chronic lymphedema.  Although lower extremity lymphedema sometimes resembles CVI (eg, discomfort, swelling), this patient's lack of risk factors for lymphatic occlusion (eg, malignancy, filariasis), relatively mild edema, and stasis dermatitis findings (eg, reddish-brown skin discoloration) make CVI more likely.

(Choice E)  Septal panniculitis containing granulomas with giant cells is characteristic of erythema nodosum (EN), a delayed hypersensitivity reaction associated with infectious, inflammatory, and autoimmune processes.  EN typically causes smooth, tender pretibial nodules.

Educational objective:Stasis dermatitis is a classic manifestation of chronic venous insufficiency and presents with reddish-brown ankle discoloration and induration.  These effects are caused by cellular extravasation from dilated veins and dermal fibrosis.​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌
